name: Licensed Needle Drop Retention
additional_sources: knowledge/research/transcripts/what not to do in editing.txt
use_when: A recognizable or especially fitting track would strengthen retention, emotion, or identity.
A section needs an energy lift, tonal reset, or memorable moment.
The platform and project allow licensed music use.
A stock track makes a serious or premium documentary sequence feel generic.
The creator wants the edit to feel premium, human-curated, and anti-filler.
The editor can audition multiple licensed tracks and time the strongest cue to a meaningful visual beat.
A CapCut/mobile edit needs music or SFX but the in-app library, screen-recorded asset, or downloaded cue has unclear rights.
avoid_when: Music rights are unclear or unsafe for the delivery platform.
The track distracts from speech, story, or brand tone.
The edit relies on the song to compensate for weak structure.
The track makes sensitive subject matter feel cheerful, cliched, or tonally disrespectful.
The song is high quality but does not describe the specific world, character, or story phase.
The music is famous or exciting but pushes the scene into the wrong ethical or emotional tone.
The track is being used to disguise slow pacing instead of enhancing a cut that already works.
The cue is available inside an app or online but its rights are not documented for the intended platform.

timeline_pattern.cue_rule: The recognizable cue should land on a story shift, reveal, emotional hit, or retention-critical section.
timeline_pattern.audition_rule: For important sections, test multiple licensed tracks against the same cut before locking the cue.
timeline_pattern.exit_rule: Plan the exit or ducking point before the track overwhelms the next story beat.
timeline_pattern.library_rule: Do not assume an in-app audio library, downloaded sound, or screen-recorded effect is cleared; record license/platform status before delivery.

motion.rule: Sync visual emphasis, cuts, or motion accents to the track only where it supports the story.
motion.avoid: Letting the song force every cut to become a music video.

sound.rule: Use licensed or platform-safe tracks and keep speech intelligible.
sound.mix: Duck music under dialogue and restore energy during visual-only or montage beats.
sound.rights: Confirm licensing before treating mainstream music, in-app library tracks, downloaded SFX, or screen-recorded effects as deliverable.
sound.tone: For war, grief, crisis, or other sensitive documentary material, prefer restraint and maturity over upbeat travel-vlog energy.
sound.quality: Premium documentary music should feel selected for taste and story identity, not dropped in as generic filler.
sound.cue_timing: Place the strongest cue, drop, or escalation on a meaningful visual turn rather than the nearest convenient cut.
sound.pace_fit: Match music energy to the speaker's pace, video rhythm, and scene tone before judging whether it improves retention.

captions.rule: If speech continues under music, captions should support intelligibility without fighting the track's visual moment.

color.rule: A music-driven section may support a stronger look, but the look should still match the surrounding edit and subject tone.

implementation.ffmpeg: Use sidechain compression or volume automation filters for dialogue ducking. Keep a rights note in project metadata or the lesson log. Use loudness checks after music changes so emotional quiet does not turn into inaudibility. Render short A/B tests for candidate tracks.
implementation.remotion: Represent the music cue as a timed audio sequence with beat, license, audition, and section markers for visual sync.
implementation.blender: Use audio markers to time motion accents if rendering animated sections.
implementation.capcut_equivalent: Use licensed music/SFX from an approved source, duplicate sections for track auditions, and manually keyframe volume under speech. Treat CapCut library audio as needing license/platform status review before final delivery.
implementation.premiere_equivalent: Use duplicate audition sequences, Essential Sound ducking or manual audio keyframes, and keep licensing notes with the project.

common_mistakes: Using copyrighted or mainstream music without rights.
Letting the needle drop bury dialogue.
Choosing a cool song that does not match the video promise.
Using cheerful or cliched stock music over serious documentary material.
Failing to plan the exit from a high-energy music moment.
Treating music quality as separate from story meaning.
Using a famous licensed track without testing whether a less obvious track fits the story better.
Locking a music-heavy edit before confirming licensing.
Choosing an upbeat track because the edit feels slow instead of tightening the timeline.
Assuming app-library music or downloaded SFX are safe because they were easy to import.
qc: Is the track licensed or platform-safe?
Does the music cue land on a meaningful moment?
Does the track improve retention or emotion rather than distract?
Does the music tone respect the subject matter?
Does the track feel intentionally selected for this world, character, or story phase?
Were serious music-led sections auditioned against at least one alternate track?
Does the strongest cue land on a meaningful visual or story beat?
Does the track fit the voice and pace of the scene rather than fighting it?
Is any in-app, downloaded, or screen-recorded audio documented as licensed, platform-safe, or temp-only?
